brief: The 5 memory patterns for AI agents — when to use vector, kv, episodic, or none at all.

slots.body: Vector, KV cache, episodic, and short-term buffers each solve different agent recall problems. Choosing the right memory tier determines latency, cost, and coherence.
Embed documents into a searchable index. The agent retrieves top-k chunks to ground answers in external knowledge.
slots.card1Body: Large knowledge bases that change infrequently and need semantic search at scale.
slots.card2Body: Chunk size and overlap directly control recall precision versus context window usage.

slots.body: Reuse key-value tensors across turns to avoid recomputing attention for prior context. Cuts latency in long multi-turn sessions.
slots.card1Body: Conversational agents with long chat histories where speed matters more than storage.
slots.card2Body: Cache eviction strategy decides the trade-off between GPU memory and context depth.

slots.body: Store agent experiences as structured events or summaries. Future turns query past episodes to personalize behavior and avoid repeated mistakes.
slots.card1Body: Personal assistants and learning agents that must accumulate user-specific lessons over time.
slots.card2Body: Without compression, episodic logs grow unbounded and slow retrieval.

slots.body: Maintain a small scratchpad of recent turns or tool outputs. It acts like RAM: fast, volatile, and tightly bound to the active context window.
slots.card1Body: Stateless APIs where you cannot persist memory server-side between requests.
slots.card2Body: Sliding window truncation silently drops older facts and breaks long references.

slots.body: Every request carries the full context in the prompt. No server-side state is stored, making scaling trivial and compliance simple.
slots.card1Body: Simple transformations, single-turn classifiers, and high-throughput microservices.
slots.card2Body: Prompt size grows linearly with history; costs explode if you simulate memory in-user.

slots.body: Match latency and retention needs to the tier. Use vector for facts, KV for speed, episodic for learning, buffers for APIs, and none for simple tasks.
slots.card1Body: Production systems that need deterministic cost and recall guarantees.
slots.card2Body: Most robust agents combine vector long-term with KV short-term caching.

slots.body: Start with the problem, not the database. The right memory pattern turns an LLM call into a coherent agent.
slots.quote: MEMORY IS WHAT SEPARATES CHATBOTS FROM AGENTS
